idiom_name: type Pricer interface { Price(qty float64) float64 } stored in a struct
implementation_notes: Go has no implements clause, so the strategy interface is satisfied implicitly and can be defined where it is consumed: the context holds an interface-typed field and never imports the concrete strategies, which is the shape the standard library uses for io.Reader and http.Handler. Define the interface next to the consumer, keep it at one method (or the few operations actually called), and let the caller supply the implementation - the selection switch then lives once at the composition root instead of running on every call. Move to the function-type variant when the strategy is a single stateless operation, because a one-method interface is heavier than a func value there.
pitfalls: A nil interface is not a nil implementation: an interface value holding a typed nil pointer is non-nil, so a nil check passes and the call panics - the classic Go interface trap.

Method sets decide satisfaction: a pointer-receiver method means only *T implements the interface, so storing a value where the context expects the interface is a compile error (and vice versa silently takes a copy).

Wide interfaces defeat the decoupling: every implementor and every test fake must grow every method, so keep the strategy interface at the operations actually called and define it beside its consumer.

variants.name: Function type / func value as the stateless strategy
variants.idiom_name: named func type (sort.Slice less func, http.HandlerFunc)
variants.implementation_notes: When the strategy is one stateless operation, Go spells it as a function type: a named type such as type Discount func(float64) float64 documents the contract, and any function or closure with that signature fits. The standard library takes this route with sort.Slice's less func and with http.HandlerFunc, which converts an ordinary function into an http.Handler. Prefer it over a one-method interface when there is no configuration to carry; switch back to the interface variant when the strategy needs state, several operations, or a named contract that mocks must implement.
pitfalls: A nil func value panics when called, exactly like a nil interface; give the context a non-nil default strategy instead of leaving the field zero-valued.

Closures capture variables by reference, so a strategy closed over a mutable config or a loop variable observes later mutations (loop variables are per-iteration since Go 1.22, other captures are not).
A struct field holding a func is not comparable and prints as a pointer; keep the field unexported behind a constructor so the expected signature is documented once.
